evidence_display: Reported by ICT 'Chief Leschi's name restored
citation: ICT 'Chief Leschi's name restored
quote: Although he refused to sign, an "X" appeared before his name
summary: The 1854 Medicine Creek treaty shows X marks by the names of Leschi and Quiemuth. Nisqually tradition and later writers (Indian Country Today) say Leschi refused to sign; others say he signed under protest. summary: The 1868 Navajo treaty was signed at Fort Sumner while the Dine were held by the U.S. at Bosque Redondo; it paid for their removal home in return for giving up territory outside the new reservation. Hunger and deaths at Bosque Redondo are in standard histories but were not checked here.

summary: Art. 4 of the 1868 Fort Bridger treaty kept the Shoshone and Bannock's right to hunt on the unoccupied lands of the United States while game remained and peace held. The Ninth Circuit held in 2023 (Northwestern Band v. Wooten) that the right is not conditioned on moving to a reservation.

summary: The 1851 Fort Laramie treaty recognized this land as territory of the Arikara, Gros Ventre and Mandan. citation: 15 Stat. 673, Art. II; 18 Stat. 291 (Kappler I 153-155), preamble
summary: The 1868 Fort Bridger treaty set this land apart for the Shoshone's 'absolute and undisturbed use and occupation'. The 1872 agreement that ceded it admits in its own preamble that mines had been found and U.S. citizens had made improvements within the reservation, before the Shoshone sold it.

citation: ICC Docket 63, 3 Ind. Cl. Comm. 313, 333 (1954); 6 Ind. Cl. Comm. 636 (1958)

summary: In ICC Docket 63 the Commission valued these 700,642 acres at 80 cents an acre ($560,513.60) as of Sept. 26, 1872, found the $27,500 paid unconscionable, and in 1954 awarded $533,013.60 less offsets; $100,000 in offsets was agreed in 1957. Money, not land, closed the claim.

citation: Lander/Brunot agreement, Sept. 26, 1872; Act of Dec. 15, 1874 (18 Stat. 291)
summary: The 1872 Brunot agreement that ceded this southern part of the Wind River reservation recites, per the atlas research, that miners and settlers were already inside it. ICC Docket 63 findings say gold was found at South Pass, including Miners' Delight, in 1868, before the reservation was set aside.

citation: Shoshone Tribe of Indians v. United States; 299 U.S. 476, 487-488 (1937)

summary: In 1878 the Indian Bureau settled the Northern Arapaho on the Shoshone's Wind River reservation without Shoshone consent; Washakie had agreed only to a short rest. In 1937 the Supreme Court held this a taking of a Shoshone property interest requiring compensation (Shoshone Tribe v. United States).

The 1868 treaty reserved this land for the Shoshone's 'absolute and undisturbed use', with other tribes admitted only if the Shoshone were willing. In 1878 the U.S. settled the Northern Arapaho there over Shoshone objection, which the Supreme Court held in 1937 was a taking of Shoshone property.

citation: United States v. Shoshone Tribe, 304 U.S. 111 (1938)
quote: That is $1.35 per acre for 1,171,770 acres, one-half of the reservation in 1878, at the time of taking.
summary: The Court of Claims valued the Shoshone half interest taken for the Northern Arapaho in 1878 at $1,581,889.50, about $1.35 an acre at 1878 values, with an increment in lieu of interest. The Supreme Court affirmed in 1938 (United States v. Shoshone Tribe). The tribe received money, not the land back.

citation: Shoshone Tribe v. United States, 299 U.S. 476 (1937), Opinion of the Court (Cardozo, J.)
quote: division of the right with strangers is an appropriation of the land pro tanto, in substance, if not in form.
summary: In 1878 the Indian Bureau settled the Northern Arapaho on the Shoshone's Wind River reservation without Shoshone consent. In Shoshone Tribe v. United States (1937) the Supreme Court held this an appropriation of an undivided half interest in the land, requiring just compensation.

citation: HistoryNet; True West; Royce 1899 entry 541
quote: President restores to public domain reservation established at Camp Grant, Nov. 9, 1871.
summary: HistoryNet and True West report that on Apr. 30, 1871 a Tucson party attacked Aravaipa and Pinal Apache families under Army protection at Camp Grant, killing about 85 to 144, mostly women and children, and taking children captive. A reserve was set apart there in Nov. 1871 and restored to the public domain in Dec. 1872.

An executive order of Nov. 9, 1871 set apart the Camp Grant reserve for the Aravaipa and Pinal Apache, months after the Camp Grant massacre. An executive order of Dec. 14, 1872 restored it to the public domain (Royce 541), the same day the San Carlos reserve was created.

evidence_display: Reported by this atlas's own data
citation: this atlas's own data
summary: An executive order of Mar. 25, 1874 set apart a Jicarilla Apache reservation on the San Juan River under an 1873 agreement Congress never ratified. An executive order of July 18, 1876 revoked it (Royce 563), so the promised reserve was not kept.

Later reductions are sequence only.

summary: The Brunot agreement's preamble records that the Utes refused in 1872 to give up any part of their reservation. PSL TREC states that federal commissioners admitted miners were trespassing in breach of the 1868 treaty but urged the Utes to cede the mines to avoid bloodshed; no primary source for that was checked.

summary: In 1875 the Los Pinos agent reported general Ute dissatisfaction with the 1873 Brunot agreement, a refusal to take payment until the boundary was settled, and insistence that they never meant to sell farming lands. PSL TREC states the southern bands felt tricked; that was not found in the agency reports.

summary: PSL TREC states most of the 1873 San Juan cession was Mouache, Capote and Weeminuche country, and that those southern bands felt tricked and accused the Tabeguache of manipulating them. The agency reports checked do not record that accusation; ARCIA 1873 notes only one Weeminuche who refused to sign.

summary: Article 6 of the 1873 Brunot agreement, which ceded this land, gave Ouray a salary of $1,000 a year for ten years, so long as he remained head chief of the Utes and at peace. Brunot reported that no presents or promises were made beyond those in the agreement itself.

citation: Report of Commissioner Felix R. Brunot, Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs 1873, pp. 93-94
quote: The execution of this order had been suspended
summary: The 1868 treaty barred unauthorized persons from ever entering this reservation. Commissioner Brunot reported in 1873 that the President had ordered miners ejected under that article, that the order was suspended, and that miners had been on the reservation in numbers for two years, before the 1873 cession.

citation: ICC Docket 327, 11 Ind. Cl. Comm. 180, 222, Findings 35, 51-53; 14 Ind. Cl. Comm. 706

summary: In ICC Docket 327 the Commission valued Royce 566 at $8,500,000 as of Apr. 29, 1874, rejecting the Ute experts' $40,773,533 mineral-land value, credited $507,662.84 paid, and entered final judgment in 1965 for $7,908,586.16. Money, not land, closed the claim.

citation: Report of Commissioner Felix R. Brunot, Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs 1873, p. 94
quote: The fact that for two years the presence of miners upon the reservation in considerable numbers was well known, and that the frequent complaints of the Indians were disregarded
summary: Commissioner Brunot reported in 1873 that miners had been on the 1868 Ute reservation in considerable numbers for two years, against the treaty's exclusion clause, and that the Utes' complaints were disregarded. The Utes had refused to sell in 1872; the San Juan cession followed in September 1873.

summary: Art. II of the 1873 Brunot agreement, which ceded this San Juan tract, provides that the United States shall permit the Utes to hunt on the ceded lands so long as the game lasts and the Indians are at peace with the white people.

summary: The 1873 agreement reserved any part of Uncompahgre Park south of the cession line, and an executive order of Aug. 17, 1876 kept a 4 by 4 mile tract as reservation. The 1884 act restored 'the lands referred to' in section 8 of the 1880 act; that these were this tract was not confirmed.

evidence_display: Reported by Fort Laramie Treaty 1868 Art. 11

summary: The 1868 Fort Laramie treaty kept a Sioux right to hunt in this Nebraska country on the Republican Fork (Art. 11). The Sioux gave it up by agreement of June 23, 1875. No source here shows the promise was broken before that.

citation: Ute Indians v. United States; Executive Order of Nov. 22, 1875; 330 U.S. 169 (1947); 1 Kappler 834 (1904 ed.)

summary: The Supreme Court records that surveyor Miller's instructions required him to stake the 1868 north line, as he admitted to the agent and the Utes, 15 to 18 miles south of the true boundary. An 1875 executive order then added land north to the first standard parallel; it was restored to the public domain in 1882.

quote: Miller's instructions, however, required him to stake out a line which he admitted to the local Indian agent and to the Utes themselves to be fifteen to eighteen miles south of the true boundary
summary: An executive order of Nov. 22, 1875 added this tract, north to the first standard parallel, to the Ute reservation after surveyor Miller's line ran 15 to 18 miles south of the true boundary. An order of Aug. 4, 1882 restored it to the public domain; the Supreme Court (1947) held the Utes had no compensable interest.

citation: United States v. Sioux Nation, 448 U.S. 371 (1980), Opinion of the Court, quoting 19 Stat. 176, 192

summary: The Aug. 15, 1876 appropriations act provided that no more subsistence would be appropriated for the Sioux unless they first gave up their rights to the hunting grounds outside the reservation, which is this Art. 16 territory, and ceded the Black Hills. The agreement of Sept. 26, 1876 then ceded it.

citation: Act of Feb. 28, 1877, ch. 72, ratifying the agreement of Sept. 26, 1876; 19 Stat. 254, 255-256 (ratifying clause and Art. 6)

summary: Article 6 of the 1876 Black Hills agreement promised a house for each principal chief if the Sioux moved to Indian Territory. Congress did not ratify that article (or the removal article) because the Sioux had not agreed to it. The PSL author calls this unlawful bribery.

evidence_display: Reported by Fort Laramie Treaty 1868 Art. 11

quote: Horn mountains shall be held and considered to be unceded Indian
summary: The 1868 Fort Laramie treaty kept this country as 'unceded Indian territory' where no white person could settle or pass without Sioux consent (Art. 16). It was ceded by the agreement of Sept. 26, 1876, confirmed in 1877. No source here shows the exclusion was breached.

citation: United States v. Sioux Nation, 448 U.S. 371 (1980), Opinion of the Court, quoting 19 Stat. 176, 192
quote: Congress enacted an appropriations bill providing that "hereafter there shall be no appropriation made for the subsistence" of the Sioux, unless they first relinquished their rights to the hunting grounds outside the reservation, ceded the Black Hills
summary: The Aug. 15, 1876 appropriations act provided that no more subsistence would be appropriated for the Sioux unless they gave up the hunting grounds and ceded the Black Hills, this area. The agreement of Sept. 26, 1876 followed, and Congress enacted it on Feb. 28, 1877.

citation: Act of Feb. 28, 1877, ch. 72, ratifying the agreement of Sept. 26, 1876; 19 Stat. 254, 255-256 (ratifying clause and Art. 6)
quote: the Government shall erect for each of the principal chiefs a good and comfortable dwelling-house" said article not having been agreed to by the Sicux Nation
summary: Article 6 of the 1876 Black Hills agreement promised a house for each principal chief if the Sioux moved to Indian Territory. Congress did not ratify that article because the Sioux had not agreed to it. The PSL author calls this unlawful bribery.

citation: United States v. Sioux Nation, 448 U.S. 371 (1980), Opinion of the Court
quote: the commission ignored the stipulation of the Fort Laramie Treaty that any cession of the lands contained within the Great Sioux Reservation would have to be joined in by three-fourths of the adult males
summary: Fort Laramie (1868) Art. 12 required three-fourths of adult Sioux men to sign any cession of the reservation. The Supreme Court records that the 1876 commission ignored that rule and the agreement was signed by only 10 percent of adult men; Congress enacted it anyway in 1877.

citation: United States v. Sioux Nation, 448 U.S. 371 (1980), Opinion of the Court
quote: the Sioux were entitled to an award of interest, at the annual rate of 5%, on the principal sum of $17.1 million, dating from 1877
summary: The Court of Claims held the 1877 act a taking of the Black Hills and awarded their 1877 value, $17.1 million, with 5 percent annual interest from 1877; the Supreme Court affirmed in 1980 (United States v. Sioux Nation). The remedy was money, not the land, and the Sioux have refused it.

citation: United States v. Sioux Nation, 448 U.S. 371 (1980), Opinion of the Court
quote: the 1877 Act effected a taking of tribal property, property which had been set aside for the exclusive occupation of the Sioux
summary: The Supreme Court held in United States v. Sioux Nation (1980) that the Act of Feb. 28, 1877, which took the Black Hills, effected a taking of tribal property set aside by the 1868 Fort Laramie treaty, requiring just compensation with interest.

citation: Act of Feb. 28, 1877 (19 Stat. 254); U.S. v. Sioux Nation, 448 U.S. 371 (1980)
summary: After United States v. Sioux Nation (1980) affirmed a money award for the Black Hills, the Sioux nations declined to accept it and continue to seek return of the land; the award remains unpaid in a Treasury account. This is widely reported; no primary source was checked here.

evidence_display: Reported by this atlas's own data
citation: this atlas's own data
summary: The Southern Ute bands were promised a San Juan River reservation in an 1878 agreement Congress never ratified. An executive order of Feb. 7, 1879 set it apart and an order of Aug. 4, 1882 restored it to the public domain (Royce 609), so the promised reserve was not kept.

citation: Testimony in relation to the Ute Indian Outbreak (1880); ARCIA 1879 Meeker telegram Sept. 10, 1879; H.R. Misc. Doc. 38, 46th Cong., 2d Sess., p. 158 and testimony of Charles Adams
quote: at the crossing of Milk Creek, right at the line of the reservation as we then understood it
summary: The 1880 agreement followed the 1879 Milk Creek fight, when troops advanced into the reservation. In 1881, when the Uncompahgre refused to leave, the agent reported they were turned over to Gen. R. S. Mackenzie's military control before they moved to Utah.

citation: ARCIA 1881, Report of the Ute Commission, Jan. 20, 1881 (signed Manypenny, Meacham, Bowman, Russell, Mears); ARCIA 1881, Report of Ute Commission pp.201-207; 21 Stat. 199-200 (three-fourths proviso)
quote: It was found that the names obtained at both agencies aggregated 581 adult male Ute Indians of the confederated bands in Colorado.
summary: Fred Conetah's history of the Northern Ute (1982), as quoted by PSL TREC, states that commissioner Otto Mears paid Utes $2 each to sign the 1880 agreement. The Ute Commission's report counts 581 adult male signatures given 'without restraint' and does not mention payments.

citation: ARCIA 1887 pp. LXXIX-LXXXII
quote: The Indian loss in this fight is said to be one man, two small girls, and an infant boy killed
summary: In August 1887 a Colorado posse burned Colorow's hunting camp, and militia and posse then attacked the camp at dawn near the Utah reservation line, killing one man, two small girls and an infant boy, the Commissioner of Indian Affairs reported. The Utes lost over 600 horses and about 2,500 sheep and goats.

citation: ARCIA 1881, Report of the Ute Commission (Uncompahgre removal); 21 Stat. 199-200; ARCIA 1881, Report of the Ute Commission (to Manypenny), pp. ~325-329
quote: We examined the land on the Grand River near the mouth of the Gunnison, and found it to be, in our opinion, unsuit- able for the Indians for agricultural or grazing purposes.
summary: The 1880 agreement promised the Uncompahgre land on the Grand River near the Gunnison if enough farmland existed there, otherwise in Utah. The commissioners judged it unsuitable and moved them to Utah. PSL TREC says the report was false; the later ICC claim (Docket 349) was settled for $300,000 without a finding.

citation: United States v. Southern Ute Indians, 402 U.S. 159, 160-161 and n. 2 (1971); 117 Ct. Cl. 433, 436 (1950)
quote: We therefore hold that the claim in this case is res judicata under the 1950 consent judgment enforcing the settlement agreement
summary: Court of Claims consent judgments in 1950 (Case No. 46640) were entered as 'full settlement and payment for the complete extinguishment' of Ute title to the western Colorado land ceded under the 1880 act; the settlements exceeded $31 million (United States v. Southern Ute, 1971). Money, not land, closed the claim.

The 1868 treaty reserved western Colorado for the Utes, and the 1880 agreement left this strip to the Southern Utes. The Hunter Act of 1895 then opened the land not allotted to entry 'under the desert, homestead, and town-site laws', while the Weeminuche moved to the western end. This happened after Royce's 1894 cutoff.

citation: United States v. Southern Ute Indians, 402 U.S. 159 (1971), Opinion of the Court
quote: The plain wording of the Act cedes to the United States all of the nonallotted acreage of the reservation, including that in the 15-mile strip (Royce Area 617) occupied by the Southern Utes.
summary: The Supreme Court held in 1971 (United States v. Southern Ute Indians) that the 1880 act ceded all nonallotted land, including this Southern Ute strip, so the 1950 Court of Claims consent judgment for the Confederated Utes barred the Southern Utes' ICC claim (Docket 328). The claim ended in money, not land.

summary: The Northern Cheyenne had no reservation of their own until the executive order of Nov. 26, 1884, about 16 years after the 1868 treaty. summary: The 1833 treaty promised 'a country and permanent home to the whole Creek nation' with a fee patent.
